**Checking Solution A (answer 1/(1−m)):** The one-big-jump heuristic is the right idea, but the count is wrong. The expected number of particles is 1/(1−m), and that includes the root. The root has no step, so only non-root particles can carry a jump. Those number Σ_{n≥1} m^n = m/(1−m) in expectation.

**Checking Solution B (answer m/(1−m)²):** This counts particles whose position exceeds x, not the first particle to cross x. Once one particle makes a large jump, all its descendants also exceed x, so this sum overcounts by roughly the mean progeny of the jumping particle. The factor n·P(X>x) for P(S_n>x) is correct, but summing it over all particles gives the wrong quantity.

**Independent check:** Let q(x) = P(M>x), and let h(x) = P(X+M'>x), where M' is an independent copy of M. Conditioning on the first generation gives P(M≤x) = G(1−h(x)), where G is the offspring generating function. Since G'(1)=m, 1−G(1−h) = m·h + O(h²). Because the stretched-exponential tail with b<1 is subexponential, P(X+M'>x) ~ P(X>x) + q(x). Therefore

q(x) ~ m(P(X>x) + q(x)), so q(x) ~ m/(1−m) · P(X>x).

For a pure path (offspring 1 with probability m, 0 otherwise), a direct sum over path lengths gives the same m/(1−m). My derivation gives the limit as m/(1−m), which matches neither proposed answer. It also has no p₀ dependence, even though the question asks for an answer in terms of p₀ and m, so I cannot rule out that the intended answer involves p₀ in a way I have missed.

Neither solution is correct as stated. Solution A's approach is closer to the right mechanism, and its error is a single factor of m. Solution B's approach double counts.

WINNER: A
